channel.title: Thirsty Planet
channel.description: Understanding water, before it's gone. The hidden water inside everyday things, the water industry in plain words, and the places already solving it.

item.title: Myth: Water Can't Run Out
item.description:
The water cycle is true. The amount of water on Earth is fixed, it has been the same for billions of years, and every drop that evaporates comes down again somewhere. From that, most people conclude that water cannot run out, and it is the most comforting mistake in the subject.
Water itself never runs out. Fresh water does: fresh water in a particular place, at a particular time, clean enough to use. The rain over the ocean is no use to a farm. The rain in a monsoon week is no use in the dry season unless something stored it. And the water under the ground, which is what half the world's irrigation now pumps, is in many places older than farming, laid down in wetter ages thousands of years ago, and refilled at a rate that has nothing to do with how fast it is being spent. The Ogallala under the American plains, the aquifers of north west India, the Nubian sandstone under the Sahara: these are being mined, and the satellites that weigh the Earth's water can watch them fall.
The cycle is real. The bank account is local, and some of the accounts are being emptied.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
The water cycle is taught to every child, and the lesson most of them take from it is that water goes round and round and can never be used up. The first part is true. The second part is the most comforting mistake in the subject, and this site exists partly to correct it. What runs out, where, and how fast.

Every child learns the water cycle. Water evaporates from the sea, rises, cools, falls as rain, runs to the river, and returns to the sea, and the diagram on the classroom wall has arrows that go round in a circle with no beginning and no end. The lesson is correct. The amount of water on the planet has been more or less the same for billions of years, and nothing that a farm, a city or a factory does can destroy a molecule of it. From this, most people draw a second conclusion, usually without noticing that they have drawn it: that water cannot run out.

It is the most comforting mistake in the subject, and one that this site spends most of its time, one article at a time, undoing. This piece is about it directly. Water as such never runs out. What runs out is water of the right kind, in the right place, at the right time, and the difference between the two is the whole of the water business.

The cycle, and the bank

The water cycle describes a flow. About 500,000 cubic kilometres of water evaporate and fall back every year, most of it over the ocean, and the flow is what keeps rivers running and aquifers filling. The flow is enormous and, over the planet as a whole, indifferent to human use. Nothing anyone does changes how much rain falls in a year by more than a rounding error.

People, though, draw on stores rather than on the flow, and the flow feeds them: rivers, lakes, soil moisture, snowpack, and, above all, groundwater. Each store has a rate at which the cycle refills it and a rate at which it is drawn down, and where the second exceeds the first, the store falls. It does not matter that the water still exists somewhere. A farmer in Kansas whose well runs dry is not consoled by the rain over the Pacific. The cycle is real, and the bank account is local.

Where the Earth's water isShare
Oceans, saltAbout 97 percent
Ice caps and glaciersAbout 2 percent
GroundwaterMost of the rest, under 1 percent
Lakes, rivers, soil, air, living thingsA few hundredths of a percent

The article on the 0.3 percent on this site walks through that table. The point of it here is the last two rows. The water people actually reach is a sliver of the total, and the largest part of that sliver is underground, where the refill rate is slow and the drawdown, since the arrival of the diesel pump, has been fast.

Old water

Most groundwater is old. A study published in 2016 that dated the world's groundwater found that only a small fraction of it, in the top layers, had fallen as rain within the last fifty years. The rest had been in the ground for centuries or millennia, and a large share of the water now being pumped for irrigation is of that kind. It was laid down in wetter ages, when the climate of the place was different, and the rain that falls there today refills it slowly or not at all. Hydrologists call it fossil water, and the name is apt: it is being extracted like coal, from a deposit that formed under conditions that no longer exist.

The Ogallala aquifer, under the Great Plains of the United States, is the best studied case. It stretches under eight states, it filled during and after the last ice age, and since the 1950s it has irrigated the maize, wheat and cattle feed of Kansas, Nebraska, Texas and Oklahoma. In the southern part, water levels have fallen by more than thirty metres, wells that once flowed have been abandoned, and the aquifer, at present pumping rates, will be effectively exhausted across large areas within decades. The rain over Kansas refills it at a few millimetres a year. The pumping takes out closer to a metre.

The same story, with different names, runs through north west India and Pakistan, where the aquifers of the Punjab have fallen fastest of any on Earth over the last twenty years, through the North China Plain, through Iran and Saudi Arabia, which pumped fossil water to grow wheat in the desert until it announced in 2008 that it would stop, and through the Nubian sandstone under the Sahara, whose water fell as rain ten thousand years ago when the desert was a savannah, and which Libya pipes north to its coastal cities through what it called the Great Man Made River.

Aquifers being minedWhere the water came fromWhat is happening
Ogallala, US High PlainsThe last ice ageDown over 30 metres in the south; decades left in places
North west India and PakistanMonsoons of past centuriesThe fastest decline measured by satellite
North China PlainPast millenniaBeijing sinking; water now piped from the Yangtze
Arabian aquifersThe wet Sahara and Arabia of 10,000 years agoSaudi wheat ended; supply now desalinated
Nubian sandstone, SaharaRain of 10,000 years agoPiped to Libya's coast; not refilling

Watching it from orbit

For most of history the state of an aquifer was known, if at all, from the wells drilled into it, which is like judging a bank account by the queue at one branch. Since 2002 a pair of satellites, called GRACE, has measured the Earth's gravity finely enough to detect the mass of water moving in and out of the ground beneath them, and their maps of the last two decades are the clearest picture of the myth failing. The regions in red, where the mass of stored water is falling year on year, are the irrigated plains of the world: north west India, the North China Plain, the Central Valley of California, the Middle East, the Ogallala. The regions in blue, gaining water, are mostly the wet tropics and the high latitudes, where nobody is short. The satellites confirm what the wells suggested, which is that water is moving, over decades, from the places that farm to the places that do not.

The other things that run out

Groundwater is the clearest case, and it is not the only one. Three other stores are being spent, and each is described elsewhere on this site.

Rivers run out at the mouth. The Colorado, the Yellow River, the Indus, the Murray and the Amu Darya of the Aral Sea article have all, in dry years or in every year, stopped reaching the sea, because the water was taken out along the way. The water cycle delivered it. The people along it spent all of it.

Snow runs out in summer. A large share of the world's farms and cities, from California to the Indus to the Andes, depend on snowpack and glaciers that store winter precipitation and release it through the dry season, and in a warming climate more of the winter falls as rain and runs off at once, and the glaciers that fed the rivers of Asia in the dry months are shrinking. The water still falls. It falls at the wrong time and does not wait.

And clean water runs out. Water that is too salty, as the brine and TDS articles explain, or too contaminated, as the arsenic and PFAS articles do, is water that exists and cannot be used, and its share is growing. A river of sewage is a river, hydrologically. It is not a supply.

What refilling looks like

A store that can be spent can be refilled, and the places that have understood the myth's failure have started to do it. Arizona has, since the 1990s, banked surplus Colorado River water in its aquifers by spreading it in basins and letting it soak in, several million acre feet of it, against the shortages now arriving. Orange County, described in its own article, refills its aquifer with treated sewage. Chennai's roofs, described in theirs, send the monsoon into the ground beneath the city. India's villages have built hundreds of thousands of check dams and recharge pits for the same purpose, and the aquifers under the districts that built most of them have, in the satellite record, begun to rise. The technique is old and simple. It is a matter of slowing water down on its way to the sea so that it soaks in, and of treating the ground as the reservoir it is. What it needs, in every case, is a decision that the store matters, made before it is empty rather than after, and that decision is easier to make in a place that has stopped believing the diagram on the wall.

What the cycle does not say

None of this contradicts the diagram on the classroom wall. The water that Kansas pumps evaporates from the maize and falls, eventually, somewhere, and the world's total is unchanged. What the diagram does not say is that the somewhere is not Kansas, that the eventually is not this year, and that the store the farmer drew from took ten thousand years to fill. The cycle is a description of the planet. Water supply is a description of a place, and a place can run out.

The useful version of the lesson, the one this site tries to teach in every article, is that water is a local budget of stores and flows, that each store has a refill rate, and that the number to know is not how much water there is but how fast the store you depend on is being refilled, and how fast it is being drawn down. In a wet country with a full river the answer is that there is plenty. On the plains of Kansas, the Punjab or the North China Plain, the answer is a date.

What it teaches

Water cannot be destroyed, and it can absolutely be used up, in the only sense that matters to anyone standing at a well. The comfort of the cycle is real and it is planetary. The problem is regional, and it is the regions that grow the food.

Ten thousand years to fill, and a few decades to spend. That is the arithmetic the diagram leaves out.

Sources

  1. Rodell, M. et al. (2018). Emerging trends in global freshwater availability. Nature 557. GRACE satellite observations of groundwater depletion in north west India, the North China Plain, the Middle East and the US High Plains.
  2. Wada, Y. et al. (2010). Global depletion of groundwater resources. Geophysical Research Letters 37.
  3. USGS, High Plains Aquifer water level monitoring: declines of over 30 metres in parts of Kansas and Texas since predevelopment.
  4. Gleeson, T. et al. (2016). The global volume and distribution of modern groundwater. Nature Geoscience 9. Most groundwater is older than 50 years; much is thousands of years old.
  5. Shiklomanov, I.A. (1993). World fresh water resources. In Gleick, P.H. (ed.), Water in Crisis. The distribution of the Earth's water.
  6. Photographs: opener: Clay cracked by L. Shyamal (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Concentric Circle Farmland (50902375916) by formulanone (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Global Freshwater Abruptly Declines (153608 - lrg) by NASA Earth Observatory image by Wanmei L (public domain) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Myth: Rain Is Pure Water
item.description:
Rain is the purest water most people will ever see. It has been evaporated by the sun, which leaves every salt and mineral behind, and it comes down with about ten milligrams of dissolved solids in a litre, against a few hundred in tap water. That is the true half of the myth.
The other half is what rain meets on the way down and where it lands. Every drop forms on a speck of dust, it washes the air of soot, pollen, sulphur and, we now know, PFAS, at levels that exceed the new drinking water limits nearly everywhere on Earth. Then it hits a roof, with its bird droppings, its moss, its lead flashing and its zinc, and runs into a gutter and a barrel, where the last of the story is written by whatever grows in the dark.
Rain is excellent water to harvest, and Chennai, Bermuda and half of rural Australia run on it. It is water to be filtered and disinfected like any other, and the sense in which it is pure is the sense that matters least to a stomach.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
Rain is distilled by the sun, and it arrives carrying almost nothing dissolved, which is the closest thing to pure water most people will ever touch. It is also the dirtiest water in the sky by the time it reaches the ground, and what happens to it on the roof and in the barrel is the whole question. Why rain is soft, what it picks up, why it is now over the PFAS limit everywhere on Earth, and how to drink it safely anyway.

Hold a glass under a downpour and what fills it is, by the measure that matters most in the water industry, the cleanest water on Earth. It has about ten milligrams of dissolved solids in a litre, which is a fiftieth of what comes from most taps and a thousandth of the sea. It was made by the sun, which evaporated it from an ocean and left every grain of salt behind, and it has never touched the ground. Rain is distilled water, falling from the sky for free, and the belief that it is pure has a long history, from the rainwater cisterns of Rome to the barrel under the gutter.

It is also, by the time it reaches the glass, carrying a sample of everything in the air it fell through and everything on the surface it landed on, and in 2022 a group of chemists concluded that rain everywhere on the planet now exceeds the strictest drinking water limit for one family of chemicals. This article is about both halves of that, because both are true, and because rain is, done properly, one of the best sources of water a house or a city can have.

The true half

The water cycle is a still. Sunlight evaporates water from the sea, from lakes, from soil and from leaves, and evaporation takes only the water. Salt, calcium, magnesium, everything the article on TDS describes, stays behind. The vapour rises, cools and condenses into cloud droplets, and the droplets grow until they fall. What arrives is, chemically, the water that a laboratory makes by boiling and condensing, and its dissolved solids, measured across the world's rain gauges, run from a few milligrams a litre inland to a few tens near the coast, where sea spray adds a little salt.

That makes rain soft, in the sense the hard water article uses. It lathers instantly, leaves no scale in a kettle, and tastes, to most people, of nothing, which is what very pure water tastes of. Places that live on rainwater, from Bermuda to the Australian outback, have soft water and no limescale, and the people who move there notice their soap goes twice as far.

Dissolved solids, milligrams per litre
Rain, inlandAbout 5 to 15
Rain, near the coastA few tens
Distilled waterUnder 1
Typical tap water100 to 500
SeawaterAbout 35,000

What it picks up on the way down

A raindrop cannot form on nothing. Every one condenses on a particle, a speck of dust, sea salt, soot or pollen, and as it falls it sweeps up more, which is why the air smells clean after a storm: the rain has washed it. What the rain washes out is what it carries down.

For most of the twentieth century the largest thing it carried was acid. Sulphur and nitrogen from coal smoke and exhaust dissolve in cloud water to make sulphuric and nitric acid, and the rain over industrial regions fell at a pH of 4, ten times more acid than clean rain's natural 5.6, killing the fish in Scandinavian and Canadian lakes and stripping the forests of central Europe. Acid rain was the first great air pollution treaty's subject, and the scrubbers on power stations that the power article mentions have raised the pH of rain over Europe and North America back towards normal since the 1990s. It is one of the environmental successes of the century, and it is a reminder that rain is exactly as clean as the air.

The air still carries soot, metals from traffic and industry, pesticides drifting from fields, and, everywhere, PFAS. The study published in 2022 by chemists in Stockholm and Zurich gathered measurements of the forever chemicals described in their own article from rain across the world, including Antarctica and the Tibetan plateau, and found PFOA and PFOS at concentrations that exceed the United States' new limit for drinking water nearly everywhere and the stricter Danish limit almost without exception. The chemicals evaporate from the sea, ride the air and come down with the rain, and they have been doing so for decades. Rain is, by the standards that now apply to a tap, contaminated before it lands, at levels of a few parts per trillion, in every country on Earth. It is a small number, and it is a fact about a substance most people still call pure.

What it picks up when it lands

The larger risk is the roof. Rain that has fallen through clean air onto a clean surface is safe to drink. Rain that has run over a roof and along a gutter into a tank is a different thing, and the difference is biology.

A roof collects, between rains, the droppings of every bird that lands on it, leaves, moss, dead insects and dust, and the first rain carries all of it into the gutter. The gutter holds standing water and rotting leaves. The tank, if it is open or badly screened, breeds mosquitoes and algae and, in warm climates, the bacteria and protozoa that make people ill. Surveys of household rainwater tanks in Australia and elsewhere find coliform bacteria in most of them and the occasional Salmonella, Giardia or Cryptosporidium, and rainwater has been traced as the source of outbreaks in every country that harvests it.

The roof also adds chemistry. Lead flashing and old lead paint leach lead. Galvanised iron leaches zinc, which is harmless at the levels found and gives the water a metallic taste. Copper roofs leach copper. Asbestos cement sheets, common on older roofs across the world, shed fibres. Bitumen and some coatings release hydrocarbons in the first years. And a roof under a flight path or beside a busy road collects whatever falls from the traffic.

What a roof adds to rain
Bird droppings, leaves, insects, dustBacteria, protozoa, organic matter, colour
Lead flashing, old paintLead
Galvanised ironZinc
Asbestos cement sheetsFibres
An open or unscreened tankMosquitoes, algae, more bacteria
A dark, cool, sealed tankVery little; the water keeps well

Drinking it anyway

None of this argues against rainwater. It argues for treating it like water, which is what the places that rely on it do.

The first flush device is the oldest and best trick. The first few millimetres of a rain carry nearly all of the roof's dirt, and a simple diverter, a vertical pipe that fills with the first flow and then lets the rest pass to the tank, throws that water away. Chennai's rules, described in the article about that city, require one on every building. A screen on the inlet keeps out leaves and mosquitoes. A sealed tank, kept dark and cool, keeps the water from growing anything. And a filter and a disinfectant, chlorine, ultraviolet light, or boiling, do for rainwater what they do for every other supply on this site, which is to make it safe from what fell in it.

Done that way, rainwater is soft, cheap, and available on every roof, and cities from Chennai to Melbourne have made it a required part of their supply, for garden and toilet use everywhere and for drinking where the tank is managed. Bermuda has drunk it for four centuries, from white limestone roofs designed to catch it, with a first flush and a cistern under every house. The World Health Organization's guidance treats it as a legitimate source with known risks, which is what it is.

The city scale

What a household does with a barrel a city can do with a plan, and the cities that have are the ones the site keeps returning to. Chennai's roofs, described in their own article, send the monsoon into the ground under the city rather than into a tank, and the water comes back through the wells filtered by the soil, which is the oldest treatment there is. Melbourne, after its own decade of drought, fitted tanks to a large share of its houses and plumbed them to toilets and gardens, which takes a tenth off the city's mains demand without anyone drinking from a barrel. Singapore catches the rain from two thirds of its island in reservoirs and treats it in plants, which is rainwater harvesting at the scale of a country. In each case the rain is collected, stored in the dark, and treated before it is drunk, and in each case it is the cheapest new water the city found. Rain is a supply. The myth is only that it needs no help.

Why the myth persists

Rain looks and tastes clean, it comes from the sky rather than a pipe, and it has been the drinking water of most of humanity for most of history, before the roof was tin and the air was full of an industrial century. The instinct that it is pure is right about its chemistry and wrong about its biology, and the two are different things, as the arsenic article said of water that passes the tests someone chose. A litre of rain has ten milligrams of minerals and, after a roof and a week in a barrel, a few thousand bacteria. It is the most distilled water most people will ever handle, and it needs a filter like everything else.

What it teaches

The myth of pure rain is the myth of the water cycle told in miniature: a true fact about the planet, that the sun distils the sea, mistaken for a fact about a glass. Rain is what the air was, and what the roof is. In a clean sky onto a clean surface it is the best water there is. In this century, under this air, on that roof, it is water, and water is what this site is for.

Ten milligrams a litre when it leaves the cloud. Everything after that is the story.

Sources

  1. World Health Organization (2017). Guidelines for Drinking water Quality, chapter on rainwater harvesting and household treatment.
  2. Cousins, I.T. et al. (2022). Outside the safe operating space of a new planetary boundary for PFAS. Environmental Science and Technology 56. PFAS in rainwater above drinking water guideline values globally.
  3. US EPA, Acid Rain Program and the National Atmospheric Deposition Program: rain chemistry and pH records since 1978.
  4. enHealth (Australia, 2010). Guidance on the use of rainwater tanks.
  5. Tamil Nadu rainwater harvesting regulations (2003) and the Chennai Metro Water guidance on first flush and storage.
  6. Photographs: opener: Rain on the roof (7635137486) by Aymeric B. from Maisons-Alfort, France (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Rainwater harvesting tank (5981896147) by SuSanA Secretariat (CC BY) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: 2024-04-26 14 46 12 A Texas Instruments tipping bucket rain gauge at the weather station at the Rutgers Gardens in North Brunswick Township, Middlesex County, New Jersey by Famartin (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Myth: Flushable wipes are flushable
item.description:
"Flushable wipes are flushable." The packet says so, the wipe goes down, and the sewer disagrees.
A flush proves nothing. Almost anything small enough will leave a toilet bowl. The question is what happens in the pipe, and the answer for most wet wipes is that nothing happens. Toilet paper is made to fall apart in water within seconds. A wipe is a nonwoven fabric, often bonded with plastic fibres, made to stay in one piece while wet, which is its whole purpose and its whole problem.
In the sewer, wipes snag, collect, and bind with the cooking fat that also should not be there, into masses that block pipes and pumps. The largest of these, found under Whitechapel in London in 2017, weighed 130 tonnes and stretched 250 metres. Britain's water companies clear around 300,000 sewer blockages a year and say most are wipes and fat.
The industry's verdict is plain: toilets are for the two things the body produces and paper. Everything else goes in the bin, whatever the packet says.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
The word on the packet is legal, and the sewer disagrees with it. What a wet wipe is made of, what happens to it after the flush, how a fatberg is built, and why the water industry has spent a decade asking for one word to be taken off the label.

In September 2017 engineers from Thames Water opened a sewer under Whitechapel in east London and found it blocked, for most of its length, by a single object. It was 250 metres long, roughly the length of two football pitches, it weighed about 130 tonnes, and it was made of cooking fat, wet wipes, nappies and everything else the residents of a busy district had put down their drains. It took nine weeks to cut out with hand tools and high pressure jets. A piece of it went to the Museum of London, where it was displayed in a sealed case and, over the months, grew a visible mould.

The Whitechapel fatberg made the word famous, and it made a technical argument public that the water industry had been having with manufacturers for a decade. The argument is about one word on a packet.

The claim

Flushable wipes are flushable. The packet says so, sometimes with a certification mark, and the claim is, in one narrow sense, true: the wipe will leave the toilet bowl when the handle is pressed. So will a sock. Flushability, as the industry means it, is about what happens next, in a pipe, a pump and a plant, and on that question the water companies of every country that has looked at it have reached the same verdict.

What a wipe is

Toilet paper is designed to fail. It is short cellulose fibre, lightly pressed, and it loses its strength within seconds of getting wet, which is why it can be flushed in quantity without ever blocking anything. That fragility is a design feature, and it took the paper industry a long time to get it right.

A wet wipe is designed to do the opposite. It has to stay in one piece while soaked in lotion for months in a packet and then survive being pulled, rubbed and wrung. It is a nonwoven fabric: fibres laid in a mat and bonded, by heat, by chemistry or by being entangled with jets of water, into a sheet that holds together wet. For most of the product's history the fibres included polyester or polypropylene, which are plastics, and which do not break down in water, in a sewer, or in a treatment plant. Wipes sold as flushable are usually made from cellulose only, regenerated or wood pulp, and are engineered to weaken over time in water, but they still hold together far longer than paper, and long enough to reach the pump.

Toilet paperA wet wipe
Made toFall apart in water within secondsStay in one piece while wet
FibresShort celluloseLong cellulose, often with plastic
Bonded byLight pressingHeat, chemistry or water jets
In the sewerGoneIntact for hours, days or longer

What happens after the flush

The article on the journey after the flush described the sewer: a network of pipes laid on a slight slope, carrying water by gravity, with pumps where the ground rises. A sewer is designed for water carrying small, soft, dispersed solids. It is not designed for sheets of fabric, and a sheet of fabric in a pipe behaves the way a sheet of fabric behaves anywhere: it catches.

It catches on the joints between pipes, on roots that have grown in, on rough brickwork in old sewers, on the impellers of pumps. Each wipe that catches makes the next one more likely to. The mass grows, and then it meets fat. Cooking oil and grease poured down kitchen sinks cools in the sewer, and, in a piece of chemistry that surprised the engineers who first analysed a fatberg, it reacts with the calcium in hard water to form a soap, in the same way that soap has always been made from fat and alkali. The soap is hard, waxy and sticks to everything, and the wipes give it a skeleton to grow on. A fatberg is, chemically, a very large bar of soap reinforced with fabric.

The evidence

The evidence is the industry's own workload. Britain's water companies clear around 300,000 sewer blockages a year, at a cost of around 100 million pounds, and they report that wipes are found in the great majority of them. Thames Water alone removes tonnes of material from its screens every day. At the treatment plant, the first thing a flush meets is a set of bars and screens, and what they catch, described in an earlier article as a monument to what people put down drains, is above all wipes. Everything caught there goes to landfill, having achieved nothing but a journey.

In 2019 the UK water industry published its own standard, Fine to Flush, with a test designed to reproduce what a sewer actually does to a product, and tested the wipes on the market against it. Most of the products labelled flushable failed. A small number, made of cellulose only and engineered to break down, passed and were allowed to carry the industry's mark. The manufacturers' own test, agreed between industry associations in Europe and America, is less demanding, and the two sides have spent a decade disputing which test describes a real sewer. The people who unblock the sewers have not found the dispute difficult.

The verdict
Wipes containing plasticNever flushable, and banned from sale in the UK from 2024
Wipes labelled flushable, cellulose onlyMost failed the water industry's own test
Wipes carrying the Fine to Flush markA small number, which the industry accepts
Toilet paperThe only thing designed for the job

The other things that should not be there

Wipes are the largest cause of blockages, and they are not the only one. Every sewer engineer has a list.

Cooking fat, oil and grease, poured down the kitchen sink while warm, are the second half of every fatberg, and they would cause blockages on their own without a single wipe. The industry's advice, to let fat cool in the pan and scrape it into the bin, is repeated on every water bill and ignored in most kitchens. Cotton buds, with plastic stems, pass every screen and end up on beaches. Sanitary products and nappies, both made to absorb water and hold together, do exactly that in a sewer. Dental floss binds. Medicines flushed away pass the plant untreated and reach the river, which is why pharmacies take them back. Cat litter, sold as flushable in some countries, sets like cement.

The pattern across the list is the same. A sewer is designed for water carrying soft, dispersed, degradable solids, and everything that is strong, absorbent, fatty or made to last defeats it.

The plastic ban

The argument about the word flushable has been running for fifteen years, and the law has begun to move on the material rather than the label. In 2024 the British government confirmed a ban on the manufacture and sale of wet wipes containing plastic, following consultations in which the water industry, the beach cleaners and the wipe manufacturers all, for once, agreed on the fibres if not on the flush. Several other countries are following. A wipe without plastic still holds together in a pipe far longer than paper, and the water industry's advice about the bin has not changed. But the plastic that made wipes indestructible, and that broke down over years into the fragments found in every river sediment tested, is on its way out of the product.

The nuance

A myth tested honestly has to say where the claim holds, and there is a small space where it does.

A wipe that is made of cellulose only, that has been engineered to lose its strength in water, and that has passed a test which reproduces a real sewer, will most likely break down before it reaches a pump, and the water industry says so by putting its own mark on it. Such products exist. They are a minority of the market, they cost more, and the packet has to be read closely. Everything else, and in particular anything that says flushable without the mark, is a wipe that will hold together in the pipe.

There is also a question of scale. One wipe, once, in a modern sewer, will probably reach the plant and be caught on the screen. The blockages are made by households that flush them every day, in old sewers, in districts that also pour fat down the sink. The problem is a habit, and the habit is what the industry is asking people to change.

The rule

The system underneath a city asks one thing of the people above it, and it is the rule the sewer engineers repeat until they are tired of it: toilets are for the two things the body produces and for paper. Wipes, cotton buds, dental floss, nappies, sanitary products, cooking fat, all of it goes in the bin, and the word on the packet does not change what happens in the pipe.

The Whitechapel fatberg was cut out, carted away and, in the end, most of it was rendered into biodiesel, which is the kind of ending the water industry likes. The next one is being assembled now, under some other street, one flush at a time.

Sources

  1. Thames Water (2017). Whitechapel fatberg: 130 tonnes, about 250 metres, cleared over nine weeks.
  2. Water UK. Around 300,000 sewer blockages a year in the UK, costing about 100 million pounds; wipes implicated in the great majority; the Fine to Flush specification (2019) and the finding that most products labelled flushable failed it.
  3. UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (2024). Ban on the manufacture and sale of wet wipes containing plastic.
  4. INDA and EDANA, Guidelines for Assessing the Flushability of Disposable Nonwoven Products, the manufacturers' test that the water industry disputes.
  5. Photographs: sewer tunnel by Martin Brechtl, Unsplash; Cesar Chu Ortega; inline: Fatberg at Museum of London by Lord Belbury (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Антистатические салфетки by Anton Diaz (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Myth: Desalination Is the Answer
item.description:
Every time a city runs short of water somebody says the answer is the sea. The sea is ninety seven percent of the water on Earth, the machines to make it fresh are proven and getting cheaper, and countries from Israel to Singapore to Saudi Arabia drink from it. I work in the industry that builds those machines, and the sentence is wrong.
The arithmetic is the first problem. All the desalination plants on Earth, running flat out, make about a hundred million cubic metres a day, which is about one percent of what the world withdraws. Seventy percent of that withdrawal is farming, and no farm can pay a dollar a cubic metre for irrigation water when a tonne of wheat sells for three hundred. Desalination supplies cities on coasts, at a price cities can bear, and it does so well. It cannot supply the Punjab.
Energy is the second, brine the third, and distance the fourth: the water is at sea level and the people who need it are, from the Atacama to the North China Plain, hundreds of kilometres inland and a thousand metres up. Desalination is one tool, for one kind of place. The rest of the toolbox is the rest of this site.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
The sea holds ninety seven percent of the water on Earth, the technology to make it fresh has existed for sixty years and its cost has fallen by two thirds, so the world's water problem is surely a matter of building enough plants. It is a comforting thought and a wrong one, for reasons of energy, brine, distance and, above all, arithmetic: desalination makes about one percent of the water people use, and the other ninety nine is mostly on farms it cannot reach.

When Cape Town approached its Day Zero, the letters to the newspapers said it. When Chennai's reservoirs emptied, the television said it. When California's reservoirs fell, the state's governor said it, and built a plant. The sea is right there, it holds ninety seven percent of the water on Earth, the technology to make it fresh has been running for sixty years and its cost has fallen by two thirds, and so, the argument goes, the world's water problem is a problem of not having built enough desalination plants. It is the most comforting sentence in the subject after the water cycle, and, like that one, it is true in the parts that do not matter.

I have spent my working life in and around the plants this article is about, and I would not be without them. This article is about why they are one tool, for one kind of place, and why the rest of the toolbox is the rest of this site.

What desalination is good at

The technology works, and the honest version of this article says so first. A modern seawater reverse osmosis plant, of the kind the desalination article describes, pushes seawater through membranes at sixty bar, takes out the salt, and delivers drinking water at about half a dollar to a dollar and a half per cubic metre, using three to four kilowatt hours of electricity to do it. Israel drinks mostly from the sea, and its five plants freed the country's natural water for its farms, as the Israel article explains. Singapore, the Gulf states, Perth, Chennai, Barcelona and San Diego all use it, and each of them is a coastal city that needed a supply that did not depend on rain, and paid for one. For that purpose, a city on a coast that can afford a dollar a cubic metre and has electricity to spare, desalination is the right answer and it is now the standard one.

The trouble begins when the sentence is extended from those cities to the world.

The arithmetic

All the desalination plants on Earth, about twenty thousand of them, have a combined capacity of around a hundred million cubic metres a day. That sounds like a great deal, and it is about 35 cubic kilometres a year. The world withdraws about four thousand cubic kilometres of fresh water a year. Desalination, at its full capacity, is under one percent of it.

The world's water, and the sea's share of it
Global freshwater withdrawalsAbout 4,000 cubic kilometres a year
Of which agricultureAbout 70 percent
Of which industry and powerAbout 20 percent
Of which cities and householdsAbout 10 percent
Global desalination capacityAbout 35 cubic kilometres a year, under 1 percent
Cost of desalinated seawaterAbout 0.5 to 1.5 dollars per cubic metre
What a farmer can pay for irrigation waterA few cents per cubic metre, often less

The second row is the one that ends the argument. Seventy percent of the world's water goes to farms, and no farm can pay for desalinated water. A tonne of wheat sells for a few hundred dollars and takes, as the bread article explains, more than a thousand cubic metres of water to grow. At a dollar a cubic metre the water would cost several times the crop. Even rice, cotton, maize and fodder, the crops that use most of the world's irrigation, are worth a fraction of what desalinated water costs to make, and the places where irrigation is emptying the aquifers, the Punjab, the North China Plain, the High Plains, the Central Valley, are hundreds of kilometres from the sea and hundreds of metres above it. Desalination can supply a city. It cannot supply the thing that uses most of the water.

Energy

A cubic metre of seawater, made fresh by reverse osmosis, takes about three to four kilowatt hours, and the older thermal plants of the Gulf take several times that. Multiply by the hundred million cubic metres a day and the world's desalination uses on the order of the electricity of a mid sized country, and in the Gulf, where most of the thermal capacity is, it is made by burning gas. Doubling the world's capacity, which the industry expects by the 2030s, doubles that. A country like Israel, with a small population and a coast, can run its supply on a few percent of its electricity. A country like India, trying to desalinate for its farms, would need more power than it has. The energy is falling, as membranes and pumps improve and as the plants are coupled to solar, and the floor is set by physics: it takes about a kilowatt hour per cubic metre simply to separate salt from seawater against the osmotic pressure, and no engineering will go below it.

Brine

For every litre of fresh water a seawater plant makes, it returns about one and a half litres of brine to the sea, at roughly twice the sea's salinity, often warmer, and carrying the chemicals used to keep the membranes clean. The brine article describes what that does and how a well designed outfall disperses it. The world's plants together produce about 140 million cubic metres of brine a day, most of it in the Gulf, a shallow, warm, nearly enclosed sea whose salinity has risen measurably since the plants were built along its shore. In an open coast with strong currents the brine is a manageable problem. In a gulf, a bay or a lagoon it is the plant's largest environmental cost, and the more plants a coast carries, the larger it grows.

Distance

The sea is at sea level. The people short of water are, more often than not, far from it and above it. Mexico City is at 2,200 metres and 300 kilometres from the coast. Tehran is at 1,200 metres and the nearest sea is the Caspian, over a mountain range. The North China Plain, the Punjab, the High Plains, the Sahel, the Central Valley: none is a coast. Lifting a cubic metre of water a thousand metres takes about three kilowatt hours, roughly what it took to desalinate it, and pumping it hundreds of kilometres takes more, so that the delivered cost doubles or triples before the water reaches the tap. The copper mines of the Atacama, described in their own article, do exactly this, lifting seawater three thousand metres to the mines, and they can because a tonne of copper is worth eight thousand dollars. A tonne of wheat is not.

Where it is going

The honest forecast for the industry, since I am in it, is growth. Capacity has doubled roughly every decade and will probably do so again, as membranes improve, as solar power makes the electricity cheap in the sunny places where the plants are, and as the coastal cities of India, China, Africa and the Americas reach the point that Chennai and Cape Town reached and decide they need a supply the rain does not control. The Gulf will keep building, the Mediterranean will build more, and the newest plants will be larger than any that exist. That growth will take the sea's share of the world's water from under one percent to perhaps two, over twenty years, in the cities that can pay. It will not reach the farms, and it will not reach inland, and every plant built will need an outfall, a power line and a tariff. The forecast is for a larger tool, used in the same kind of place, and the sentence at the top of this article will be as wrong in 2045 as it is now.

What the sentence leaves out

The sentence is comforting because it makes the problem technical, and technical problems have vendors. The places on this site that solved their water did not, for the most part, solve it with the sea. Singapore desalinates, and it also catches its rain, recycles its sewage and fixes its leaks. Israel desalinates, and it also drips its crops, reuses its wastewater and prices its water. Las Vegas has no desalination plant and has cut its river use by a quarter while growing by half. Orange County drinks its own sewage. Tokyo found a city's worth of water in its pipes. Every one of those is cheaper per cubic metre than the sea, and every one is available inland. The myth's harm lies in what it excuses: it lets a city, or a country, put off the cheaper and harder things, on the promise of a plant.

What the sea can and cannot do
Supply a coastal city that can pay a dollar a cubic metreYes, and it does
Replace a river or an aquifer for a city inland and uphillAt several times the cost, rarely
Supply irrigation for staple cropsNo, at any foreseeable price
Reduce the water a city needsNo; that is pricing, leaks and reuse
Make water without energy or brineNo; the floor is physics

The version that is true

There is a sentence about desalination that is right, and it is worth setting down beside the wrong one. For a coastal city that has done the cheaper things first, that has fixed its leaks, priced its water, reused its sewage and caught its rain, and that still needs a supply that does not depend on the sky, the sea is the next source, and it is now affordable, reliable and clean. Every city in this series that built a plant on those terms, Perth, Singapore, Israel's coast, has been glad of it. The cities that built one instead of the cheaper things, or that promised one and put off the rest, are the ones that will build a second plant and a third and still be short, because the demand a plant is built to meet is the demand the city never reduced. The sea is a good last answer. It is a poor first one.

What it teaches

Desalination is real, it works, and it is the right answer for a growing number of coastal cities, which is why my industry keeps building it. It is also under one percent of the world's water and cannot become much more, because most of the world's water is on farms that cannot pay for it and are nowhere near the sea. The world's water problem is, as every article on this site has said in its own way, a problem of how much is spent and where, and a plant on the coast changes neither. The sea is the answer to a particular question, asked by a particular kind of city. It is not the answer to the question.

One percent, at full capacity, from a sea that holds ninety seven.

Sources

  1. International Desalination Association and Global Water Intelligence, DesalData: global installed capacity of about 100 million cubic metres a day across some 20,000 plants.
  2. Jones, E. et al. (2019). The state of desalination and brine production: a global outlook. Science of the Total Environment 657. Brine volumes of about 1.5 litres per litre of product.
  3. FAO AQUASTAT: global freshwater withdrawals of about 4,000 cubic kilometres a year, about 70 percent for agriculture.
  4. Voutchkov, N. (2018). Energy use for membrane seawater desalination: current status and trends. Desalination 431. About 3 to 4 kilowatt hours per cubic metre.
  5. Israel Water Authority, share of domestic supply from desalination, and Sorek and Hadera plant costs of around 0.5 dollars per cubic metre.
  6. Photographs: opener: 160810-N-FP878-007 (28801419432) by Commander, U.S. Naval Forces Europe-Afri (public domain) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Wheat farm located along Clark Rd in Pasco by Araceli Fuentes (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Reuven Rivlin in a visit at IDE - Sorek Desalination Plant (0097) by Mark Neyman (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Myth: Boiling water removes everything
item.description:
"If in doubt, boil it." Good advice, and it covers half of what can be wrong with water.
Boiling kills. One minute at a rolling boil, three at altitude, and every bacterium, virus and parasite in the water is dead, including the Cryptosporidium that chlorine cannot touch. That is why a boil water notice is the right response to a burst main or a failed filter, and why boiling has saved more lives than any other water treatment in history.
Boiling does not remove anything. Salt, nitrate, lead, arsenic, pesticides, the fluoride in the tap and the dissolved solids that make the kettle fur: all of it stays in the pan, and since some of the water leaves as steam, what remains is slightly more concentrated than before. The scale in the kettle is the proof. It is the dissolved minerals, made visible by the heat, and none of them went anywhere.
Two problems, two tools. Microbes: boil. Chemistry: a filter, a membrane, or a different source. The kettle only ever solved the first.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
A rolling boil is the oldest water treatment there is, and it does one job perfectly: it kills. What boiling does to the microbes, what it leaves untouched, what it makes slightly worse, and why a boil water notice and a lead pipe warning are asking for two different things.

When a water main bursts and the utility issues a boil water notice, it is relying on the oldest treatment there is. Boiling has been used to make water safe since before anyone knew what was in it, and it has probably saved more lives than every chlorination plant put together. It is also the source of a belief that goes well beyond what the kettle can do: that boiled water is clean water, full stop. This article separates the two claims, because one of them is true and the other, in the situations where it matters most, is the opposite of true.

The claim

Boiling water removes everything. Stated as a household rule, and applied, in practice, to any water that seems doubtful: cloudy water, water after a flood, water in a country with an unfamiliar tap, water from an old pipe.

What boiling does perfectly

Boiling kills. Bacteria, viruses and the protozoa that cause waterborne disease are living things with proteins that unfold at temperatures well below the boiling point, and a rolling boil finishes the job on all of them. Cholera, typhoid, the E. coli of a contaminated well, hepatitis A, norovirus, Giardia and, importantly, Cryptosporidium, the parasite whose tough cyst shrugs off chlorine and made 400,000 people ill in Milwaukee in 1993, as the disinfection article recounts: all of them die in a pan.

Boiling water for safety
At sea levelBring to a rolling boil and hold for one minute
Above about 2,000 metres, where water boils coolerHold for three minutes
Cloudy waterLet it settle or strain it through cloth first, then boil
AfterwardsCool covered, store in a clean container, use within a day

This is why a boil water notice is the right response to a burst main, a failed filter or a flood, all of which can let microbes into a supply that is otherwise safe. It is why travellers are told to boil, and why the advice has held for a century in every language. Against the biology of water, the kettle is as good as a treatment plant.

What boiling leaves untouched

Boiling removes nothing. That is the half of the rule that fails, and it fails in the situations where people most often reach for the kettle.

Everything that is dissolved in water stays dissolved when the water boils, because boiling only changes the water. Salt stays. Nitrate from fertiliser stays. Fluoride stays. The metals that come from pipes and from the ground, lead, copper, arsenic, stay. Pesticides and industrial chemicals stay, apart from the few that are volatile enough to leave with the steam. The dissolved solids described in the article on TDS stay, all of them, which is the point of that article: nothing catches a dissolved substance except a membrane, a resin or distillation, and a saucepan is none of those.

What boiling does and does not do
Bacteria, viruses, parasitesKilled
Salt and dissolved mineralsUntouched, and concentrated
NitrateUntouched, and concentrated
Lead, copper, arsenic and other metalsUntouched, and concentrated
Pesticides and most industrial chemicalsMostly untouched
ChlorineDriven off, which removes the taste and the protection
Cloudiness from particlesNot removed, unless the water settles

What boiling makes slightly worse

Worse than untouched, in fact, because some of the water leaves. A pan at a rolling boil loses water as steam, and what stays behind holds all of the dissolved substances in less water. Boil a litre down to nine tenths and every dissolved concentration has risen by a tenth. It is a small effect, and it is in the wrong direction, and for water that is doubtful because of its chemistry rather than its biology, boiling makes it marginally worse while creating a feeling of safety that is entirely false.

The kettle proves it. The scale that builds on the element is calcium and magnesium that were dissolved in the water and came out of solution when it was heated, as the hard water article explains. They were in the water before, invisible. Boiling did not remove them; it made them visible, in the kettle, and left the rest in the cup. A person who boils hard water to purify it is looking at the evidence that it does not work every time they descale.

Two notices, two problems

The clearest way to see the difference is in the two warnings a water utility issues, which sound alike and ask for opposite things.

A boil water notice follows a microbial risk: a burst main that let groundwater in, a positive test for E. coli, a failure at the disinfection stage, a flood. It says: the biology of your water may be unsafe, boil it, and the advice is complete. Boiling fixes the problem entirely.

A do not drink notice, or a lead warning of the kind that Flint's residents should have received in 2014, as the pH article recounts, follows a chemical risk: lead from pipes, a chemical spill upstream, nitrate above the limit, arsenic in a well. It says: the chemistry of your water is unsafe, and boiling will not help. The water needs a filter certified for the substance, a different source, or bottled water until the cause is fixed. Boiling lead contaminated water, as the American environmental agency's guidance says plainly, does not remove the lead and can increase its concentration.

NoticeThe problemThe fix
Boil waterMicrobes: burst main, failed disinfection, floodBoil for one minute
Do not drinkChemistry: lead, nitrate, arsenic, a spillA certified filter, another source, or bottled water

Distillation, which is not boiling

There is a way to make boiling remove things, and it is the one people are half remembering when they trust the kettle. If the steam is caught and condensed, the water that results is distilled, and it has left everything dissolved behind in the pot. Distillation is how the first desalination plants made fresh water from the sea, as the desalination article recounts, and it is what a solar still does: a dark tray of dirty water under a sloping sheet of glass, with the sun evaporating the water and the glass condensing it into a channel. A survival still of that kind makes a litre or two a day, and the water is pure enough to be flat and tasteless, because the minerals that give water its taste were left behind with the salt. The kettle boils but does not condense, and that is the whole difference. The steam that carries pure water away is the steam that fogs the kitchen window.

Filters, and what each one removes

For the chemistry that boiling cannot touch, the household tools are filters, and they are not all the same.

A jug filter with activated carbon removes chlorine, which improves the taste, and some organic compounds, and it reduces lead and copper if the cartridge is designed to and is changed on time. It removes no nitrate, no salt and no fluoride. An under sink reverse osmosis unit, a small version of the membrane described in its own article, removes nearly everything dissolved, including nitrate, salt, fluoride and metals, and produces a stream of concentrate to the drain as its larger cousins do. A ceramic or hollow fibre filter removes microbes without chemicals, and is the traveller's alternative to boiling. None of them is a kettle, and the kettle is none of them. The cheapest way to know which is needed is the utility's published results for the tap, which say what is in the water before anyone decides how to treat it.

Why the belief is so strong

The rule survives because it was once the whole truth. For most of human history the dangers in water were living, and the kettle answered them. Cholera, typhoid and dysentery killed more people than any chemical in a pipe, and the advice to boil was the difference between an outbreak and a quiet summer, in every army camp, every city slum and every colonial household with a servant and a stove. The chemical problems of water, lead, nitrate, arsenic, industrial solvents, arrived later, with the industries that made them, and they arrived in cities whose biology had already been fixed by the treatment plant. The belief is a survivor from the age before the plant, and it is right about that age. It is only in the age after, when the tap is safe from microbes and the remaining risks are dissolved, that the kettle's reputation exceeds its powers.

The nuance

The rule holds, entirely, for the problem it was made for. Where water is doubtful because of what might be living in it, which is the case in most of the world and in most emergencies, boiling is the best available treatment, and the advice to boil is the advice that saves lives. Nothing in this article should make anyone hesitate to boil water they suspect.

It fails for the problem that a modern city's water is more likely to have. In a city with a working treatment plant and a chlorine residual, the microbes are handled, and the risks that remain are old pipes, industrial chemistry and the ground the water came through, none of which the kettle touches. In that setting, boiling tap water for safety achieves nothing except driving off the chlorine that was protecting it, and a person worried about lead from their own plumbing is better served by running the tap for a minute in the morning and fitting a filter than by boiling anything.

Two problems, two tools

Water can be unsafe in two ways, and the ways need different tools. Living things are killed by heat, and the kettle kills them all. Dissolved things are removed only by a membrane, a resin, or distillation, and the kettle removes none of them. The oldest water treatment in the world does its one job perfectly and has been asked, for centuries, to do a second one that it cannot. The scale on the element has been trying to say so all along.

Sources

  1. World Health Organization, Guidelines for Drinking water Quality, and WHO technical brief on boiling water: a rolling boil is sufficient to inactivate pathogenic bacteria, viruses and protozoa.
  2. US Centers for Disease Control, guidance on boil water advisories: one minute at a rolling boil, three minutes above 2,000 metres.
  3. US EPA, guidance on lead in drinking water: boiling does not remove lead and may increase its concentration.
  4. Photographs: opener: Person pours water from yellow kettle in wooden kitchen by Shixart1985 (CC BY) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: 2008-07-05 Water boiling in cooking pot by Ildar Sagdejev (Specious) (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Billycan-campfire (cropped) by Flickr user "Johan Larsson" (CC BY) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Myth: A bath uses more water than a shower
item.description:
"A shower uses less water than a bath." It depends, and the modern shower has quietly overturned the rule.
A full standard bath holds about 80 litres, and a large one 150. A typical shower head delivers 8 to 10 litres a minute, so a five minute shower is 40 to 50 litres and a bath wins by nothing. A power shower delivers 15 litres a minute or more, and ten minutes under one is 150 litres, a large bath. The average shower in Britain lasts seven to eight minutes, which puts it, at a typical head, level with a bath.
The line is easy to find. Time the shower, put a bucket under the head for a minute to measure the flow, and multiply. Under 80 litres and the shower wins. Over it and the bath was the economical choice all along.
The water is the smaller half of it. Heating that water is the largest energy use in most homes after the heating itself, and every litre of hot water, bath or shower, was heated by gas or electricity.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
Everyone knows a shower saves water. The numbers say it depends on the shower head, the minutes and the size of the bath, and that the modern power shower has quietly overturned the rule. What a bath and a shower actually use, how to know which side of the line you are on, and why the water is the smaller half of the story.

Of all the water advice that everyone has absorbed without checking, the rule that a shower uses less water than a bath is the most confidently repeated. It was true when it was coined, in an age of trickling electric showers and deep enamel baths, and it is the reason a generation of people feel virtuous under the shower and guilty in the tub. The numbers have moved since. This article measures both, finds where the line falls, and then points out that the water was never the larger half of the question.

The claim

A shower uses less water than a bath. Stated as a rule, without conditions, and usually followed by a suggestion that a bath is an indulgence.

What a bath holds

A standard bath, the kind fitted in most European homes, holds about 80 litres when filled to a normal bathing depth, and up to about 120 if filled to the overflow. A large or deep bath holds 150 or more. A shallow bath, run for a child, might be 40. The volume is fixed by the bath and the depth, and it does not change with how long the person stays in it, which is the bath's quiet advantage.

BathLitres
Shallow, for a childAbout 40
Standard, filled to bathing depthAbout 80
Standard, filled to the overflowAbout 120
Large or deep bath150 or more

What a shower uses

A shower's water is its flow rate multiplied by its minutes, and both vary more than most people realise.

An old style electric shower, heating water as it passes through a small element, delivers 4 to 6 litres a minute, which is the trickle the rule was built on. A modern mixer shower, fed from a hot water cylinder or a combination boiler, delivers 8 to 10. A power shower, with a pump, delivers 13 to 16 or more, and the large rainfall heads sold for luxury bathrooms can pass 20. The minutes are the other half: surveys in Britain put the average shower at about seven and a half minutes, and teenagers, as every parent knows, at considerably more.

ShowerLitres a minuteFive minutesEight minutesTwelve minutes
Electric showerAbout 5254060
Mixer shower8 to 1040 to 5065 to 8095 to 120
Power shower13 to 1665 to 80105 to 130155 to 190
Large rainfall headUp to 20100160240

Where the line falls

Put the two tables together and the rule dissolves.

A five minute shower under any head uses less than a standard bath. An eight minute shower under a mixer, which is the average British shower under the commonest kind of head, uses about 80 litres, which is the bath. An eight minute power shower uses more than the bath, and a twelve minute one under a rainfall head uses three baths. The shower wins clearly only when it is short, or the head is modest, and it loses clearly when it is long and the head is generous, which describes a great many modern bathrooms.

The verdict
Short shower, any headThe shower wins
Average shower, mixer headLevel with a bath
Average shower, power showerThe bath wins
Long shower, any modern headThe bath wins, sometimes by a lot

The verdict, then, is that it depends, and that the modern shower has quietly overturned a rule that was written for a different appliance. A person who takes long showers under a power shower and feels virtuous about skipping baths has the sums the wrong way round.

How to know which side you are on

The line is easy to find at home, with a bucket and a watch.

Put a bucket under the shower head, run the shower as you normally would, and time how long it takes to collect ten litres; a bucket usually has a mark. Divide, and that is the flow rate in litres a minute. Then time an ordinary shower, from turning on to turning off. Multiply the two, and compare with 80. Under it, the shower is the economical choice. Over it, the bath was, all along, and the cheaper fix is a shorter shower or a lower flow head rather than a change of habit.

Low flow shower heads, which mix air into the water to keep the feel of a full spray at 6 to 8 litres a minute, are the single most effective change, and they cost a few tens of euros. A shower timer, of the kind Cape Town's households used in 2018 as the Day Zero article describes, is the second. The city that cut its water use in half did it largely by cutting its showers to two minutes, which is 20 litres under any head.

The larger half of the story

Water is the smaller half of a bath or a shower, and it is worth saying so in an article about water.

Every litre of hot water in a home was heated, by gas, oil or electricity, from the temperature of the mains to about forty degrees, and heating water is the largest use of energy in most homes after heating the rooms, somewhere around a sixth of the household's total. A litre of hot water costs far more in energy than in water, and it carries a carbon cost that the water itself does not. So the question of bath against shower, honestly asked, is about hot litres, and the answer is the same as before: fewer minutes and a lower flow head save more than any choice between the two fixtures.

There is also the water's journey, which the rest of this series describes. Every litre that went down the bath or shower drain is greywater, lightly used and warm, and in a house with the plumbing for it, described in the greywater article, it would have flushed the toilet before it left.

The rest of the bathroom

The bath and the shower are the largest uses of water in a home, and they are not the only ones, and the rest of the room is worth measuring while the bucket is out.

The toilet is the second largest, at around a quarter of household water. An old cistern uses 9 to 13 litres a flush; a modern dual flush uses 4 to 6, and swapping one for the other saves more than most changes to showering. A running tap delivers about 6 litres a minute, so brushing teeth with the tap open for two minutes uses 12, which is a short shower's worth every morning and evening. A washing machine uses around 50 litres a cycle, a dishwasher around 10 to 15, and both use less than the same job done by hand under a running tap. A dripping tap loses several litres a day, and a leaking cistern, which is common and silent, can lose hundreds.

The rest of the home, per useLitres
Old toilet cistern, per flush9 to 13
Modern dual flush, per flush4 to 6
Tap running, per minuteAbout 6
Washing machine, per cycleAbout 50
Dishwasher, per cycle10 to 15
A person in Britain, per day, all usesAbout 140

A person in Britain uses about 140 litres a day at home, of which the bathroom is well over half. Cape Town's households, in 2018, lived on 50. The gap between the two numbers is almost entirely the shower and the toilet, and the bucket, the timer and the dual flush cistern are the whole of the difference.

The bath's other trick

A bath has one more property that the rule never mentions: its water is still there when the bather gets out. Eighty litres of warm, lightly soapy greywater sits in the tub, and in a house with a garden, a bucket and a little patience, it waters the beds, rinses the paths or, as Cape Town's households found in 2018, flushes the toilet for the rest of the day. A shower's water is gone down the drain the moment it has done its work. Neither fact changes the arithmetic of the rule, but a bath that is used twice is, on the day, the more economical of the two by a wide margin, and in a drought it is the one the water industry quietly recommends.

Where the rule came from

The rule dates from the 1970s and 1980s, when the electric shower arrived in British and European bathrooms as a cheap alternative to a hot water cylinder, and it was true of that appliance: a small element could heat only a trickle, four or five litres a minute, and a five minute wash under it used a quarter of a bath. The water companies and the energy campaigns of the period repeated it, reasonably, and it entered the culture. The mixer shower, the combination boiler and then the pumped power shower followed over the next thirty years, each delivering more water than the last, and the rule was never revised. It is a good example of advice that was measured once, for one appliance, and repeated for forty years about a different one.

The nuance

The rule holds in some cases. It is right for the appliance it was written for: a short shower under a modest head against a full bath. It was right for most bathrooms in 1980. It is wrong for a great many bathrooms in 2026, and it is wrong in a way that flatters the person breaking it.

A bath is a fixed 80 litres, decided by the bath. A shower is a variable, decided by the head and the person, and it can be 20 litres or 250. That is the whole finding. The bath does not deserve its reputation, and the shower does not deserve its halo; the number is in the minutes, and the bucket will tell you what yours is.

Sources

  1. Waterwise (UK) and the Energy Saving Trust, At Home with Water (2013): bath volumes, shower flow rates, average shower duration of about seven and a half minutes, and hot water as a share of household energy.
  2. Energy Saving Trust: typical mixer shower 8 to 10 litres a minute; power showers 13 to 16 litres a minute or more; a standard bath about 80 litres.
  3. European Commission ecodesign and water label data: flow rates of shower heads and taps.
  4. Photographs: opener: High speed shower filtered by turydddu @ Flickr, retouched by JovanCormac (CC BY) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Bathtub of Khan Pool Suite in Amantaka luxury Resort & Hotel in Luang Prabang Laos by Basile Morin (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Itron Water Meter by Ganesh Dhamodkar (CC BY) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Thirsty: Wine
item.description:
Almost every farmer on Earth is trying to get more water to their crop. Winemakers are the strange exception. They spend their careers trying to make the plant a little thirsty.
A vine with plenty of water grows big, watery grapes and lots of leaves. A vine that has to work sends its roots down and produces small grapes with concentrated flavour, which is what ends up tasting like something. Growers call the technique deficit irrigation, and in parts of Europe the rules go further: several famous appellations simply forbid irrigation, on the grounds that a vineyard that needs watering is planted in the wrong place.
All of which makes the number a little awkward. A glass of wine still carries about 109 litres of water, and per litre wine costs roughly three times what beer does. Grapes are not especially thirsty; there just are not many of them per bottle, and the vine drinks rain all season either way.
The part worth watching is what heat is doing to those old rules. Regions that built their identity on never irrigating are facing summers their vines were not planted for, and some of the bans have quietly started to bend.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
Almost every farmer on Earth is trying to get more water to their crop. Winemakers are the exception, spending their careers keeping the vine a little thirsty. A glass of wine still carries about 109 litres, three times what beer does per litre, and the old rules about not watering vines are starting to bend in the heat.

Walk through a vineyard in August in the south of France and the ground between the rows is bare and cracked, the leaves are small, and the vines look, to anyone used to a garden, as if somebody has forgotten to water them. Nobody has forgotten. In most of the famous wine regions of Europe the vines are not watered on purpose, and for a long time it was against the rules to water them at all. Wine is the one crop on this site whose growers spend their careers keeping the plant slightly thirsty, and that makes its water footprint an odd one to read.

A hundred and nine litres

By the Water Footprint Network's method, wine comes to about 869 litres of water per litre in the global average, counting the rain the vines took up, the irrigation applied where there was any, and the clean water it would take to dilute the pollution from the vineyard and the winery. A 125 millilitre glass is a seventh of that, about 109 litres.

StageLitresShare
Growing the grapes10092%
Winery cleaning65%
The bottle and the rest33%

The split is approximate; the total is the citable figure. As with everything on this site that grows, the vineyard is nearly all of it, and the winery, where the water goes on washing tanks, barrels and floors, is a small share.

Per litre, wine costs roughly three times what beer does, at 869 litres against 298. Grapes are not especially thirsty as fruit go, at around 600 litres per kilogram, well below an avocado. The difference is concentration: it takes somewhere between 1.2 and 1.5 kilograms of grapes to make a bottle of wine, where a litre of beer needs less than 200 grams of grain, and the water follows the fruit.

The vine wanted less

Here is the fact that sets wine apart from every other footprint in the series. A vine with plenty of water grows a big canopy of leaves and large, watery grapes, and the wine made from them is thin. A vine that has to work for its water sends its roots deep, sets fewer and smaller grapes, and concentrates sugar, acid and flavour into them, and that is the wine that ends up tasting like something. The plant, mildly stressed, makes a better product.

Growers have known this for centuries, and the modern name for managing it deliberately is deficit irrigation: giving the vine less water than it would take if offered, at the stages of the season when a little stress improves the fruit, and enough at the stages when it would only do harm. In the New World, in California, Australia, Chile and Argentina, most vineyards are irrigated and the deficit is managed with a valve. In much of Europe the deficit is managed by planting the vine in a place where the rain is a little short, and leaving it to cope.

What water does to a vine
Plenty of waterLarge canopy, big watery grapes, thin wine
A managed shortageDeep roots, small concentrated grapes, better wine
Too littleStalled ripening, lost crop

That is why the vineyard in August looks neglected. The bare ground and the small leaves are the point.

The rule that forbade watering

In the appellation system that governs the classic wine regions of France, and in the similar systems of Italy and Spain, the vine's thirst was written into law. For most of the twentieth century French rules prohibited irrigating vines during the growing season in appellation vineyards, on the principle that a vineyard which needed watering was planted in the wrong place, and that the character of a wine came from the land and the weather it was given rather than from a pipe. Several of the most famous appellations kept, and still keep, outright bans.

The result is a wine footprint that, in Europe, is almost entirely green. The vine drinks what falls on it, over a season, from the soil, and the 869 litres per litre in the global average is mostly rain on a hillside that was going to be rained on regardless. Irrigated New World vineyards carry a blue share, drawn from rivers in dry valleys, and it is worth knowing which bottle came from where.

Where the world's wine grows, and on what

The global average hides two different industries. The old wine countries of Europe, France, Italy and Spain, still make around half the world's wine, mostly in temperate or Mediterranean climates where winter rain stores enough moisture in the soil to carry an unirrigated vine through summer, and where the rules described above kept the pipes out. Their footprint is green almost to the last litre.

The newer wine regions were planted where the sun was reliable and the rain was not. The vineyards of Australia's Murray Darling basin, of California's Central Valley, of Chile's central valleys and of Argentina's Mendoza, a desert at the foot of the Andes, produce wine of every quality, and nearly all of it on irrigation drawn from rivers and aquifers that other users, cities and other crops among them, also depend on. In a drought year the competition is direct. During Australia's long drought of the 2000s the price of water rights in the Murray Darling basin rose until some growers found it paid better to sell their water than to make wine with it, and the vineyards that survived were the ones with the deepest pockets or the oldest rights.

Where wine growsWhat the vines drink
The classic European regionsWinter rain stored in the soil, and the rules forbid much else
Australia, California, Chile, Argentina, South AfricaIrrigation from rivers and aquifers, managed by deficit
Cooler new regions, New Zealand, Oregon, EnglandMostly rain

A bottle from Bordeaux and a bottle from Mendoza can carry a similar number of litres, and in one case they fell from the sky onto a field that would have been rained on anyway, and in the other they were pumped from a river in a desert. As with every product on this site, the label's most useful line, for water, is the one that says where.

Grapes per bottle

The arithmetic that makes wine three times beer is worth a moment, because it is not about the plant being thirsty. A vine uses water roughly the way any fruit tree does, and grapes at around 600 litres per kilogram are middling among fruits. The multiplier is yield. A bottle of wine needs between 1.2 and 1.5 kilograms of grapes, crushed and pressed, and the skins, seeds and stems, a quarter of the weight, are left behind as pomace. A litre of beer needs under 200 grams of barley. Wine simply contains more crop per glass, and the deficit irrigation that makes it taste of something lowers the yield further, concentrating the water along with the flavour.

The winery

The winery's water is a small share and a familiar story. Grapes are crushed, the juice or the must is fermented in tanks, the wine is racked from vessel to vessel, aged, filtered and bottled, and every tank, hose, press and barrel is washed between uses, because grape sugar feeds every microbe that would spoil a wine as readily as the yeast that makes it. A winery uses somewhere between two and six litres of water for every litre of wine, nearly all of it cleaning, and the water that leaves carries sugar, yeast and lees, and is treated like a brewery's or a dairy's, increasingly by digestion into biogas. Harvest is the pressure point: a winery may crush its whole year's fruit in six weeks, and its water use and its effluent peak with it.

The rule is starting to bend

The part of the story worth watching is what heat is doing to the old rules. Regions that built their identity on never irrigating are facing summers their vines were not planted for: longer droughts, higher temperatures, ripening that races ahead of flavour, and in the worst years vines that simply stop. France permitted irrigation under conditions in 2006 and has extended the derogations in drought years since. Individual appellations have loosened their own rules through the 2010s and 2020s, allowing drip lines to be laid in vineyards where a decade earlier they would have cost a grower the right to use the name on the label.
